report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with DB pool contention
report.summary: Between 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 and API error rate increased while traffic stayed near baseline. Slow traces largely show time spent waiting on DB connection acquisition in inventory.reserve, with dependency metrics showing increased pool pending and stable DB CPU.

findings.text: From 14:15–14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 rose 420ms→2840ms and API error rate 0.3%→6.8%, while request rate stayed near ~120 rps (API error rate only).
In a representative slow trace, most time is in inventory.reserve with db.pool.acquire taking 2190ms; 18/20 slow sampled traces show pool waits >1800ms (sampled-slow scope only).
A release at 14:12 changed the inventory client connection pool max 20→5; latency rise begins at 14:15, which is temporally consistent but not proof of causality.
Dependency metrics show pool pending requests increased 0→84, while DB CPU stayed ~36% (baseline 34%) and payment authorization p95 stayed ~140ms (baseline 135ms).

nextSteps: Collect time-series of inventory client pool acquire latency, active/idle connections, and pending counts by instance for 14:00–14:30 to verify contention scope beyond the 20 sampled slow traces.
Request the service owner to validate the release diff and confirm whether the 20→5 pool-max change applied broadly (all pods/canary) and whether any other connection settings changed at 14:12.
With inventory/checkout service-owner approval, run a controlled pool-size experiment (e.g., restore prior max or step up) and measure impact on pool waits, checkout p95, and API error rate.
report.uncertainty: Evidence localizes delays to DB connection acquisition in sampled slow traces and rising pool pending, but does not prove all traffic is affected or that the pool-max change is the sole factor. No controlled experiment or cohort comparison is included.
report.customerUpdate: We’re seeing elevated checkout latency and API errors during 14:15–14:30 UTC, with traces indicating delays are largely from waiting to acquire database connections in inventory.reserve. This is consistent with connection pool contention; payments and DB CPU appear stable. Next we’ll validate pool metrics scope, confirm release configuration reach, and—only with service-owner approval—run a controlled pool-size experiment to measure impact.

evidence.title: Checkout latency and errors rose
evidence.detail: From 14:15 to 14:30 UTC, checkout-api p95 increased from 420ms baseline to 2840ms; error rate rose from 0.3% to 6.8%. Request rate stayed near 120 requests/second. This is API error rate, not measured lost orders or revenue.

evidence.title: Most sampled time is waiting for a DB connection
evidence.detail: Representative trace trc_checkout_241: POST /checkout 2840ms; inventory.reserve 2520ms; db.pool.acquire 2190ms; SELECT inventory 180ms; payments.authorize 130ms. 18 of 20 slow sampled traces have pool waits above 1800ms. Samples do not prove all requests behave the same way.

evidence.title: Pool limit changed during the release
evidence.detail: At 14:12 UTC checkout release 8f2c1d changed the inventory client connection pool maximum from 20 to 5. The latency increase starts at 14:15. Temporal correlation supports a hypothesis but does not establish causality.

evidence.title: Database CPU and payment time stayed stable
evidence.detail: Database CPU is 36%, baseline 34%. Payment authorization p95 is 140ms, baseline 135ms. Pool pending requests rose from 0 to 84. These observations favor pool contention over a payment-provider slowdown or database CPU saturation.

evidence.title: No controlled mitigation has been measured
evidence.detail: There has been no rollback, load test, pool-size experiment, or measured revenue-impact analysis. No writes or remediation are authorized. A human must approve any operational change.

report.title: Checkout slowdown consistent with payment provider timeouts
report.summary: During the query window, checkout p95 and error rate increased while request rate stayed stable across old and new releases. Sampled slow traces commonly show payments.authorize dominating latency with upstream HTTP 504s, consistent with a payment-provider or network path issue, but provider-side confirmation is missing.

findings.text: Metrics show checkout p95 rose 460ms→3210ms and errors 0.4%→8.2% at 15:18 UTC, with stable request rate and similar impact across old/new release cohorts.
In 20 slow sampled traces, 17 include slow payments.authorize; one representative trace shows payments.authorize 2880ms with an upstream HTTP 504 dominating a 3210ms checkout.
A presentation-only deploy occurred at 15:10 UTC, but errors starting 15:18 UTC also affect the old release, which is counter-evidence for a code-regression limited to the new version.

Inventory latency and DB pool indicators appear normal in the measured metrics (pool pending 0, DB CPU 33%, inventory 150ms near 145ms baseline), reducing support for inventory/DB as the bottleneck in sampled data.

nextSteps: Collect payment-service metrics during the window (authorize latency distribution, HTTP status breakdown including 504s, and timeout counts) and compare to a prior baseline period.
Request the payment provider’s incident/status confirmation and any available request/timeout logs for the same UTC interval, and validate correlation with the sampled 504 traces.

With payment-service owner approval, run a controlled, reversible timeout and dependency-health diagnostic (read-only where possible) to localize whether failures originate in provider response vs network path.
report.uncertainty: Evidence localizes latency to payments.authorize only for 20 sampled slow traces; it does not quantify overall 504 frequency or prove provider responsibility. Provider-side telemetry/status is unavailable, and normal DB/inventory metrics cannot exclude all downstream issues.
report.customerUpdate: We’re seeing elevated checkout latency and errors in the measured window, affecting both old and new releases. Sampled slow traces indicate payment authorization is frequently the dominant delay and includes upstream 504s, which is consistent with a provider or network-path issue, but provider confirmation is not yet available. Next we will gather payment-service status-code/timeout metrics, request provider-side evidence for the same interval, and—only with service-owner approval—run a controlled diagnostic to better localize the dependency.

evidence.title: Payment errors rose across both release cohorts
evidence.detail: Checkout p95 increased from 460ms to 3210ms and errors from 0.4% to 8.2% at 15:18 UTC. Old and new application versions show similar error rates and latency. Request rate is stable.

evidence.title: Payment authorization dominates the slow trace
evidence.detail: Trace trc_payment_242: checkout 3210ms; inventory.reserve 150ms; db.pool.acquire 18ms; payments.authorize 2880ms with upstream HTTP 504. 17 of 20 slow sampled traces have slow payment authorization.

evidence.title: A deploy occurred before the alert
evidence.detail: At 15:10 UTC a presentation-only release changed the checkout receipt label. Errors begin at 15:18 and affect the old release too. A nearby deploy alone is not sufficient evidence of a regression.

evidence.title: Inventory and DB pool metrics are normal
evidence.detail: Pool pending requests are 0; database CPU is 33%; inventory latency is 150ms, baseline 145ms. The external payment provider has not yet confirmed an incident.

evidence.title: Provider-side evidence is unavailable
evidence.detail: No provider-side traces or confirmed provider status report. Do not claim a confirmed root cause, recommend blindly retrying charges, or claim that a rollback will solve the problem.

report.title: Checkout latency elevated; dependency unknown
report.summary: Aggregate checkout p95 latency and API error rate increased within the queried window, but missing child spans prevent localizing slowness to inventory, database, payments, or network. Two simultaneous changes exist without per-cohort or dependency metrics, so the leading hypothesis cannot be selected from evidence.

findings.text: Observed symptom: checkout p95 rose from 440ms to 1920ms and API error rate from 0.4% to 4.1% in aggregate checkout metrics only.
Tracing coverage gap: collector sampling/config fault omitted child spans for inventory, database, and payments, leaving only the root span and no dependency attribution.
Two changes occurred at 16:12 UTC (checkout release and network-policy update) with no per-cohort or dependency measurements to distinguish their effects.
No order-completion or revenue measurements are available, so impact cannot be translated into financial loss from this bundle.

nextSteps: Collect read-only dependency health signals during the same interval (inventory, database, payments, network policy drops/denies) and compare to a prior baseline window.
Restore or validate trace/collector configuration so checkout requests emit child spans for inventory, database, and payments, with service-owner approval before any telemetry configuration change.
With service-owner approval, segment metrics by release cohort and by network-policy version to test whether latency/error changes align with one change more than the other.
report.uncertainty: This bundle shows aggregate checkout regression but lacks downstream spans and per-cohort segmentation; simultaneous changes and missing dependency metrics prevent even a supported leading hypothesis about which component is driving latency/errors.
report.customerUpdate: We see an increase in checkout latency and API errors in aggregate metrics, but current tracing is missing downstream spans, so we cannot yet attribute slowness to inventory, database, payments, or network. Next, we propose collecting dependency health signals, restoring tracing (with owner approval), and comparing metrics by change cohort to narrow the likely source.

evidence.title: The checkout symptom is real
evidence.detail: Checkout p95 increased from 440ms to 1920ms; API error rate increased from 0.4% to 4.1%. Only aggregate checkout metrics are available.

evidence.title: Downstream trace coverage is missing
evidence.detail: A collector sampling/configuration fault omitted child spans for inventory, database, and payments. The root span is present but does not identify which dependency is slow.

evidence.title: Two simultaneous changes are uncorroborated
evidence.detail: Both a checkout release and a network-policy update occurred at 16:12 UTC. There are no per-cohort metrics or dependency measurements to distinguish them. The evidence is insufficient to select a cause.

evidence.title: Impact has not been translated into revenue
evidence.detail: There are no order-completion or revenue measurements. Do not invent financial loss. Restore telemetry and collect comparative evidence before recommending a specific mitigation.
